Draft:

Summer Projects Should Belong to Students

Every June, many schools send students home with a summer project meant to keep their minds from going slack over the break. The goal is sound. Ten weeks without reading, writing, or problem solving can erase a surprising amount of what students learned during the year. The real question is who should design these projects. I believe students should design their own summer projects, with teachers setting broad expectations and offering guidance. Student-designed projects produce more genuine effort, build skills that classrooms rarely teach, and make learning feel like something students own rather than something done to them.

The first reason is motivation. A teacher-designed project, such as a required report on an assigned novel, is often finished the night before school starts, rushed and resented. Summer is the one stretch of the year when students have real control over their time, and an assignment that feels like more homework competes poorly with everything else. A project a student chose is different. A girl who loves baking might study the chemistry of why bread rises, testing different amounts of yeast and recording the results. A boy obsessed with basketball might track his free-throw percentage across a summer and learn to graph and analyze the data. Because these projects grow out of real interests, students return to them willingly, and that willingness is exactly what keeps learning alive over the break.

Second, designing a project is itself a valuable lesson. During the school year, teachers decide almost everything: what to read, what questions to answer, when work is due. Students rarely practice planning a long task, setting goals, or adjusting when something fails. When a student must pick a question, figure out how to answer it, and manage the work over several weeks, he or she is practicing the independence that college and jobs demand. A student whose garden experiment dies in July has to figure out what went wrong and try again. No worksheet teaches that kind of persistence.

Third, student-designed projects respect the fact that students are different. A single teacher-designed assignment assumes every student needs the same practice and shares the same interests. In reality, one student may need to strengthen her writing while another is ready to tackle an advanced coding project. Letting students choose allows each of them to work at the edge of their own ability instead of the average of the class.

Critics argue that students, left to themselves, will choose projects that are too easy or skip the work entirely. This concern is fair, but it argues for guidance, not teacher control. Teachers can require a short proposal before summer begins, set standards for how much work is expected, and ask for a final presentation in the fall. With that structure, freedom and accountability work together.

Summer projects exist to keep curiosity alive. Nothing does that better than letting students pursue what they already care about.
